title: Latino Americans separate intergenerational progress from belief that the American dream is attainable
source_unit: Pew Research Center National Survey of Latinos

denominator.unit: Latino adults in Pew National Survey of Latinos; weighted survey estimates

observations.method: Bilingual, nationally representative survey of Latino adults; respondents selected among achieved, on the way, out of reach, and does not exist.
observations.uncertainty: The categories measure reported cultural judgment, not a standardized mobility threshold or observed income/wealth trajectory.
observations.counterinterpretation: A respondent can reject the dream while experiencing material progress, or view it as out of reach while improving relative to parents.

denominator.unit: Latino adults in Pew National Survey of Latinos; weighted survey estimates

better_than_parents.unit: percent saying own standard of living is better than parents' at same age

children_better.unit: percent expecting children's standard of living to be better than their own

observations.method: Retrospective and prospective self-assessments in the same national survey; comparison is descriptive and not a linked income panel.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived standard of living may reflect expectations, reference groups, household composition, prices, migration histories, and memory as well as material change.
observations.counterinterpretation: Positive family mobility assessments do not establish current affordability, wealth accumulation, housing access, or actual future outcomes.

observations.period: October 6-16, 2025; immigrant versus US-born Latino mobility and attainability judgments

denominator.unit: Latino adults; subgroup estimates by nativity

observations.method: Pew nativity and generation subgroup comparison using source-defined immigrant and US-born categories.
observations.uncertainty: Nativity contrasts are descriptive; age, arrival cohort, legal status, language, family resources, place, and selection are jointly structured.
observations.counterinterpretation: The contrast does not show that migration causes optimism or that nativity determines political or consumer behavior.

observations.period: October 6-16, 2025; open-ended meaning of the American dream

denominator.unit: Latino adults; open-ended responses coded into overlapping themes

financial_economic_homeownership.unit: approximately percent mentioning financial security, economic opportunity, or homeownership

observations.method: Open-ended response coding; categories can overlap and percentages do not sum to 100.
observations.uncertainty: Thematic coding reflects source categories and respondent language; it does not measure intensity, causal priority, or later action.
observations.counterinterpretation: Material and relational meanings can coexist; no single coded theme is a complete definition of the dream.

related_sources.claim: Working-class self-identification supplies a neighboring status-meaning comparison across income, education, work type, stress, and party.
Current national economic evaluations provide a separate judgment context and should not be substituted for mobility meaning.

boundary: This record measures reported American-dream meaning, perceived intergenerational living-standard change, and nativity subgroup differences. It does not measure causal income mobility, wealth, housing purchase, legal status, voting, political action, consumer switching, or future outcomes.
